title: Like, dislike and desire
subtitle: fancy, be keen on, loathe, long for
summary: Express liking, disliking and wanting with the right strength - fond of, keen on, fall for, loathe, be appalled by, long for and dread.

lesson.heading: Liking someone
lesson.text: A whole family of verbs describes growing to like someone. You may **quite like** a person at first, then **fancy** them, then **fall in love with** them or **fall for** them.

examples.text: I **quite liked** him when we first met, but I didn't really **fancy** him in any big way.
examples.note: fancy someone = find them sexually attractive; informal

examples.text: He **fascinated** me with his stories of his travels, and something mysterious about his past **attracted** me.
Little by little I **fell in love** with him.
I can't see why I didn't **fall for** him the moment we met.

lesson.heading: Liking things and people - and the preposition that follows
rows: His sense of humour **appealed to** me.
I was **captivated by** his smiling eyes.
He's **fond of** animals and small children.
He's **passionate about** the things he believes in.
He **cares for** the people around him.
I hope we'll always be as **devoted to** each other as we are now.
lesson.note: A **caring** person is one who thinks about other people's feelings and needs.

lesson.heading: Strong ways of saying dislike
lesson.text: **Loathe**, **detest**, **despise**, **cannot stand** and **cannot bear** are all stronger ways of saying dislike. They are followed by a noun or an -ing form.

examples.text: I **can't bear listening** to her stupid stories.

lesson.heading: The negative effect something has on you
lesson.text: **Repel**, **revolt**, **appal** and **disgust** describe the strong negative effect something has on a person. Note that they usually appear in the passive when you talk about the person.

examples.text: I was **revolted by** the way he spoke.
We were **appalled by** the conditions in the refugee camp.

lesson.note: If something is disgusting or fascinating, you feel disgusted or fascinated - never ~~I felt disgusting~~.

lesson.heading: Wanting and dreading
rows: a formal word for wish, or a sexual wish for someone
I have a strong **desire to** see the Himalayas before I die.
think about something in the future with pleasant anticipation
I'm **looking forward to going** to Fiji.
the opposite of look forward to; rather strong
After this long, cold winter, I'm **longing for** spring.
a more poetic way of saying long for
He will never stop **yearning for** his country.
lesson.note: Look forward to and dread are both followed by a noun or an -ing form: looking forward to starting the job, not ~~to start~~.

lesson.text: The noun desire takes to + infinitive: a strong desire to find out, not ~~a desire of finding out~~.

exercises.prompt: Mrs Williams is very fond ___ her son-in-law.
Are you keen ___ rugby? There's a big match on TV tonight.
exercises.explanation: You are keen on an activity.

exercises.prompt: Spending a whole day with my cousins doesn't appeal ___ me.
We just looked at each other and we fell ___ love immediately.
She's so beautiful. I fell ___ her the moment I saw her.
exercises.explanation: Fall for someone means suddenly fall in love with them.

exercises.prompt: Our grandmother was always very affectionate ___ us and hugged us every time she saw us.
She's very passionate ___ wildlife and helps at the local animal rescue centre.
exercises.explanation: You are passionate about a cause.

exercises.prompt: Jack and Lily are very devoted ___ each other.
exercises.explanation: Devoted to means loyally and lovingly attached.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with a sentence that means almost the same.

pairs.left: Do you think Ethan is attractive?

pairs.right: She's keen on rowing and golf.
I can't bear very salty food.

exercises.prompt: Which person probably feels more strongly?
options: He's very fond of his sister.
exercises.explanation: Devoted to is stronger than fond of.

exercises.prompt: Which person probably feels more strongly?
exercises.explanation: Loathe is a much stronger word than dislike.

exercises.prompt: Which person probably feels more strongly?
exercises.explanation: Yearn is the more poetic and more intense of the two.

exercises.prompt: Which person probably feels more strongly?
options: I'm not really looking forward to the exam.
exercises.explanation: Dread is a strong word; not looking forward to is mild.

exercises.prompt: I was ___ by the terrible conditions in the prison. They were simply inhuman.
exercises.explanation: Appal describes the shock a terrible situation causes; use it in the passive about the person.

exercises.prompt: I can't bear selfish people. I ___ anyone who never considers others.
exercises.explanation: Despise is a strong way of saying dislike; dispose is a different word altogether.

exercises.prompt: Her manner ___ me at first, but now I've begun to like her more.
exercises.explanation: Repel describes the strong negative effect someone has on you.

exercises.prompt: I felt a strong desire ___ out what had happened to my old school friends.
exercises.explanation: The noun desire is followed by to + infinitive, not of + -ing.

exercises.prompt: Are you looking forward to ___ your new job?
exercises.explanation: Look forward to is followed by a noun or an -ing form.

exercises.statement: I felt absolutely disgusting by his unkind remarks about Sylvia.
exercises.explanation: False - I felt absolutely disgusted by his unkind remarks. If something is disgusting, you feel disgusted.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression show liking, disliking or wanting?
